P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

An object is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Which values should be substituted in the mirror formula?

New Cartesian Sign Convention (Topic 4). Why it applies: both the object and the focus of a concave mirror lie in front of it, on the left of P.

Treats both distances as plain lengths. uuu is never positive for a real object.
f=+10f = +10f=+10 cm is the sign for a convex mirror.
Object on the left → uuu negative; F of a concave mirror is in front (left) → fff negative.
Both signs reversed.

Given: concave mirror, f = 10 cm; object 20 cm in front. Asked: the signed values of uuu and fff.

Concept used: New Cartesian Sign Convention (Topic 4). Why it applies: both the object and the focus of a concave mirror lie in front of it, on the left of P.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Treats both distances as plain lengths. uuu is never positive for a real object.
    • (b) ✘ f=+10f = +10f=+10 cm is the sign for a convex mirror.
    • (c) ✔ Object on the left → uuu negative; F of a concave mirror is in front (left) → fff negative.
    • (d) ✘ Both signs reversed.

  2. Check: with (c), 1v=−110+120=−120\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{10} + \dfrac{1}{20} = -\dfrac{1}{20}v1​=−101​+201​=−201​, so v=−20v = -20v=−20 cm: a real image at C for an object at C — exactly what the image table says ✔.

  3. Answer (c)

P2● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which ray-diagram rule for a convex lens is correct?

the three easy rays for lenses (Topic 6). Why it applies: each option describes one ray.

After refraction a parallel ray passes through the focus on the other side, F2F_2F2​.
A ray through O goes straight on, undeviated.
A ray through F1F_1F1​ emerges parallel to the axis — the parallel-ray rule run backwards.
No such rule. A ray from B passing through 2F12F_12F1​ does not, in general, go through F2F_2F2​. (Only rays from a point object on the axis at 2F12F_12F1​ meet again at 2F22F_22F2​.)

Given: four statements about rays through a convex lens. Asked: the correct one.

Concept used: the three easy rays for lenses (Topic 6). Why it applies: each option describes one ray.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ After refraction a parallel ray passes through the focus on the other side, F2F_2F2​.
    • (b) ✘ A ray through O goes straight on, undeviated.
    • (c) ✔ A ray through F1F_1F1​ emerges parallel to the axis — the parallel-ray rule run backwards.
    • (d) ✘ No such rule. A ray from B passing through 2F12F_12F1​ does not, in general, go through F2F_2F2​. (Only rays from a point object on the axis at 2F12F_12F1​ meet again at 2F22F_22F2​.)

  2. Check: (c) is ray 2 of the Topic 6 table ✔.

  3. Answer (c)

P3● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which pair is correct for a spherical mirror?

"mirror plus, lens minus" for the formula; "mirror minus, lens plus" for magnification (Topic 4, Topic 7). Why it applies: the two devices use different signs.

This is the lens pair.
Mirror formula, but lens magnification.
Mirror formula and mirror magnification.
Lens formula with mirror magnification.

Given: four formula pairs. Asked: the mirror pair.

Concept used: "mirror plus, lens minus" for the formula; "mirror minus, lens plus" for magnification (Topic 4, Topic 7). Why it applies: the two devices use different signs.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ This is the lens pair.
    • (b) ✘ Mirror formula, but lens magnification.
    • (c) ✔ Mirror formula and mirror magnification.
    • (d) ✘ Lens formula with mirror magnification.

  2. Check: for a plane mirror (v=−uv = -uv=−u), (c) gives m=+1m = +1m=+1 — virtual, erect, same size ✔.

  3. Answer (c)

P4● FoundationNumerical · 1 markOriginal

Find the power of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm.

Full solution

Given: convex lens, f = 20 cm. Asked: power PPP.

Concept used: P=1fP = \dfrac{1}{f}P=f1​ with fff in metres; convex → positive (Topic 7). Why it applies: power is defined only with fff in metres.

  1. 1

    Convex lens → fff positive: f=+20f = +20f=+20 cm.

  2. 2

    Convert to metres (divide by 100).

    f=+0.20 mf = +0.20\ \text{m}f=+0.20 mSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Write the definition.

    P=1fP = \dfrac{1}{f}P=f1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Substitute.

    P=1(+0.20 m)P = \dfrac{1}{(+0.20\ \text{m})}P=(+0.20 m)1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Divide.

    P=+5 DP = +5\ \text{D}P=+5 DSwipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: 15 D=0.2\dfrac{1}{5\ \text{D}} = 0.25 D1​=0.2 m = 20 cm ✔.

  7. Answer P=+5 DP = +5\ \text{D}P=+5 D

    Common trap: 120=0.05\dfrac{1}{20} = 0.05201​=0.05 D — the result of leaving fff in centimetres (100 times too small).

P5● FoundationFill in the blank · 1 markOriginal

Fill in the blanks: A ray of light passing obliquely from glass into air bends ________ the normal, because its speed ________.

Full solution

Given: a ray going from glass into air at an angle. Asked: direction of bending and the speed change.

Concept used: bending depends on the change of speed (Topic 5). Why it applies: air is optically rarer than glass.

  1. 1

    Air has a smaller refractive index than glass, so light is faster in air.

  2. 2

    Going from glass to air, light speeds up.

  3. 3

    A ray that speeds up bends away from the normal.

  4. Check: this is what happens at the second face of a glass slab (Topic 5) ✔.

  5. Answer away from; increases

    Common trap: "towards; increases" — the speed is right but the direction is reversed.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P6● FoundationTrue/False with justification · 1 markOriginal

True or false? "The image formed by a concave lens can be obtained on a screen if the object is placed far enough away." Justify.

Full solution

Given: a claim about concave-lens images. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: a concave lens always forms a virtual image (Topic 6). Why it applies: only real images can be caught on a screen.

  1. 1

    A concave lens always spreads light out, so refracted rays never meet.

  2. 2

    Its image is therefore always virtual, whatever the object distance.

  3. 3

    Virtual images cannot be caught on a screen.

  4. Check: both rows of the concave-lens table say "virtual, erect" ✔.

  5. Answer False. A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image, which cannot be obtained on a screen.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P7● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

Why does a dentist use a small concave mirror to look at a patient's teeth?

Full solution

Given: a dentist's mirror. Asked: why a concave mirror is used.

Concept used: a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image when the object is between P and F (Topic 2). Why it applies: the mirror is held close to the tooth.

  1. 1

    The mirror is held close, so the tooth is between P and F.

  2. 2

    The image is then enlarged and erect.

  3. Check: the same idea as a shaving mirror ✔.

  4. Answer The tooth lies between the pole and the focus, so the concave mirror forms an enlarged, erect (virtual) image, letting the dentist see the tooth in detail.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P8● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which of these quantities has a unit?

ratios of like quantities have no unit; power is 1f\dfrac{1}{f}f1​ (Topic 5, Topic 7). Why it applies: three options are ratios.

Ratio of two speeds — no unit.
Ratio of two heights — no unit.
1metre\dfrac{1}{\text{metre}}metre1​ → dioptre (D).
Ratio of two sines — no unit (it equals the refractive index).

Given: four optical quantities. Asked: the one with a unit.

Concept used: ratios of like quantities have no unit; power is 1f\dfrac{1}{f}f1​ (Topic 5, Topic 7). Why it applies: three options are ratios.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Ratio of two speeds — no unit.
    • (b) ✘ Ratio of two heights — no unit.
    • (c) ✔ 1metre\dfrac{1}{\text{metre}}metre1​ → dioptre (D).
    • (d) ✘ Ratio of two sines — no unit (it equals the refractive index).

  2. Check: D = m⁻¹, which is a real unit ✔.

  3. Answer (c)

P9● FoundationDiagram-based · 2 marksOriginal

Draw a ray diagram to show the image of the Sun formed by a concave mirror. State the position, size and nature of the image.

Full solution

Given: object at infinity (the Sun); concave mirror. Asked: ray diagram; image description.

Concept used: rays from a very distant object arrive parallel; a concave mirror converges parallel rays through F (Topic 2). Why it applies: the Sun is effectively at infinity.

  1. 1

    How to draw it

    Draw the principal axis and a concave mirror (back shaded); mark P, F and C with PF = FC.

  2. 2

    Draw two or three rays parallel to the principal axis coming from the left (arrowheads pointing towards the mirror).

  3. 3

    Reflect each so that it passes through F (arrowheads after reflection).

  4. 4

    Mark the meeting point F as the image: a bright point.

  5. Check: this is Activity 9.2 — the burning spot forms at F ✔.

  6. Answer Image at the principal focus F; highly diminished (point-sized); real and inverted.

    Common trap: Drawing the rays meeting at C. Parallel rays meet at F.

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P10● FoundationDiagram-based · 2 marksOriginal

Draw a ray diagram for an object placed in front of a convex mirror. Describe the image.

Full solution

Given: convex mirror; object at a finite distance. Asked: ray diagram and description.

Concept used: ray 1 (parallel → appears from F) and ray 3 (aimed at C → back along itself) for a convex mirror (Topic 3). Why it applies: both reflected rays diverge, so the image comes from their backward extensions.

  1. 1

    How to draw it

    Draw the axis and the convex mirror; mark P, and F and C behind the mirror (PF = FC).

  2. 2

    Draw the object AB in front of the mirror.

  3. 3

    Ray 1: from B parallel to the axis; reflect it away from the axis; extend it back to F as a dashed line.

  4. 4

    Ray 3: from B towards C; it reflects back along itself; extend it behind the mirror to C, dashed.

  5. 5

    The dashed lines meet at B′, between P and F. Draw A′B′ dashed and upright.

  6. Check: convex-mirror rule: virtual, erect, diminished, between P and F ✔.

  7. Answer Image behind the mirror between P and F; diminished; virtual and erect.

    Common trap: Marking F in front of the convex mirror.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P11●● StandardNumerical · 3 marksOriginal

A 2 cm tall object is placed 14 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.

Full solution

Given: concave mirror, f = 10 cm; object 2 cm tall at 14 cm. Asked: vvv, h′h'h′, nature.

Concept used: mirror formula 1v+1u=1f\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}v1​+u1​=f1​ and m=−vu=h′hm = -\dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{h'}{h}m=−uv​=hh′​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: uuu, fff and hhh are known.

  1. 1

    Sign table.

    Quantity Value Reason for the sign
    uuu −14 cm-14\ \text{cm}−14 cm object in front
    fff −10 cm-10\ \text{cm}−10 cm concave mirror
    hhh +2 cm+2\ \text{cm}+2 cm upright object
    vvv ? to be found
    h′h'h′ ? to be found
  2. 2

    Rearrange the mirror formula.

    1v=1f−1u\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}v1​=f1​−u1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Substitute.

    1v=1(−10 cm)−1(−14 cm)\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{(-10\ \text{cm})} - \dfrac{1}{(-14\ \text{cm})}v1​=(−10 cm)1​−(−14 cm)1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Minus of a minus becomes plus.

    1v=−110 cm+114 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{10\ \text{cm}} + \dfrac{1}{14\ \text{cm}}v1​=−10 cm1​+14 cm1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    LCM of 10 and 14 is 70.

    1v=−7+570 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{-7 + 5}{70\ \text{cm}}v1​=70 cm−7+5​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Add.

    1v=−270 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{2}{70\ \text{cm}}v1​=−70 cm2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    Simplify.

    1v=−135 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{35\ \text{cm}}v1​=−35 cm1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Flip.

    v=−35 cmv = -35\ \text{cm}v=−35 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Mirror magnification.

    m=−vum = -\dfrac{v}{u}m=−uv​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Substitute.

    m=−(−35 cm)(−14 cm)m = -\dfrac{(-35\ \text{cm})}{(-14\ \text{cm})}m=−(−14 cm)(−35 cm)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Minus ÷ minus inside is plus; the front minus remains.

    m=−2.5m = -2.5m=−2.5Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Use h′=m×hh' = m \times hh′=m×h; substitute.

    h′=(−2.5)×2 cmh' = (-2.5) \times 2\ \text{cm}h′=(−2.5)×2 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Multiply.

    h′=−5 cmh' = -5\ \text{cm}h′=−5 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →

  14. Check: 1(−35)+1(−14)=−2−570=−110\dfrac{1}{(-35)} + \dfrac{1}{(-14)} = \dfrac{-2 - 5}{70} = -\dfrac{1}{10}(−35)1​+(−14)1​=70−2−5​=−101​ ✔. Object between F (10 cm) and C (20 cm) → image beyond C, real, inverted, enlarged ✔.

  15. Answer v=−35 cmv = -35\ \text{cm}v=−35 cm, h′=−5 cmh' = -5\ \text{cm}h′=−5 cm — 35 cm in front of the mirror; 5 cm tall; real, inverted and enlarged.

    Common trap: Getting v=+5.8v = +5.8v=+5.8 cm by using f=+10f = +10f=+10 cm.

P12●● StandardNumerical · 3 marksOriginal

A convex mirror has a radius of curvature of 60 cm. A 5 cm tall object is placed 20 cm in front of it.
(a) Find the position and size of the image.
(b) A student took f=−30f = -30f=−30 cm. Work out what he would get, and explain why his answer must be wrong.

Full solution

Given: convex mirror, R = 60 cm; object 5 cm tall at 20 cm. Asked: (a) vvv and h′h'h′; (b) the result with the wrong sign, and why it is impossible.

Concept used: f=R2f = \dfrac{R}{2}f=2R​, positive for a convex mirror; mirror formula; m=−vum = -\dfrac{v}{u}m=−uv​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: the sign of fff decides whether the result describes a convex mirror at all.

  1. 1

    (a)

    Focal length: convex → positive; f=R2f = \dfrac{R}{2}f=2R​.

    f=+60 cm2f = \dfrac{+60\ \text{cm}}{2}f=2+60 cm​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Divide.

    f=+30 cmf = +30\ \text{cm}f=+30 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Sign table.

    Quantity Value Reason for the sign
    uuu −20 cm-20\ \text{cm}−20 cm object in front
    fff +30 cm+30\ \text{cm}+30 cm convex mirror
    hhh +5 cm+5\ \text{cm}+5 cm upright object
    vvv ? to be found
    h′h'h′ ? to be found
  4. 4

    Rearrange.

    1v=1f−1u\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u}v1​=f1​−u1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Substitute.

    1v=1(+30 cm)−1(−20 cm)\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{(+30\ \text{cm})} - \dfrac{1}{(-20\ \text{cm})}v1​=(+30 cm)1​−(−20 cm)1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Minus of a minus becomes plus.

    1v=130 cm+120 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{30\ \text{cm}} + \dfrac{1}{20\ \text{cm}}v1​=30 cm1​+20 cm1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 7

    LCM 60.

    1v=2+360 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{2 + 3}{60\ \text{cm}}v1​=60 cm2+3​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Add.

    1v=560 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{5}{60\ \text{cm}}v1​=60 cm5​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 9

    Simplify.

    1v=112 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{12\ \text{cm}}v1​=12 cm1​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 10

    Flip.

    v=+12 cmv = +12\ \text{cm}v=+12 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 11

    Magnification.

    m=−vum = -\dfrac{v}{u}m=−uv​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  12. 12

    Substitute.

    m=−(+12 cm)(−20 cm)m = -\dfrac{(+12\ \text{cm})}{(-20\ \text{cm})}m=−(−20 cm)(+12 cm)​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 13

    Signs give plus.

    m=+0.6m = +0.6m=+0.6Swipe to see the whole equation →
  14. 14

    h′=m×hh' = m \times hh′=m×h; substitute.

    h′=(+0.6)×5 cmh' = (+0.6) \times 5\ \text{cm}h′=(+0.6)×5 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  15. 15

    Multiply.

    h′=+3 cmh' = +3\ \text{cm}h′=+3 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →
  16. 16

    (b)

    With the wrong sign, f=−30f = -30f=−30 cm, substitute: 1v=1(−30 cm)−1(−20 cm)\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{(-30\ \text{cm})} - \dfrac{1}{(-20\ \text{cm})}v1​=(−30 cm)1​−(−20 cm)1​.

  17. 17

    Minus of a minus: 1v=−130 cm+120 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{30\ \text{cm}} + \dfrac{1}{20\ \text{cm}}v1​=−30 cm1​+20 cm1​.

  18. 18

    LCM 60: 1v=−2+360 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{-2 + 3}{60\ \text{cm}}v1​=60 cm−2+3​.

  19. 19

    Simplify: 1v=160 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{60\ \text{cm}}v1​=60 cm1​.

  20. 20

    Flip: v=+60v = +60v=+60 cm.

  21. 21

    Magnification: m=−(+60 cm)(−20 cm)m = -\dfrac{(+60\ \text{cm})}{(-20\ \text{cm})}m=−(−20 cm)(+60 cm)​.

  22. 22

    Simplify: m=+3m = +3m=+3 — a virtual image 3 times enlarged.

  23. 23

    A convex mirror always forms a diminished image, so an enlarged image is impossible. The wrong sign of fff turned the convex mirror into a concave one.

  24. Check: (a) 112+1(−20)=5−360=130\dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{(-20)} = \dfrac{5 - 3}{60} = \dfrac{1}{30}121​+(−20)1​=605−3​=301​ ✔; image between P and F (12 cm < 30 cm), diminished ✔.

  25. Answer (a) v=+12 cmv = +12\ \text{cm}v=+12 cm (behind the mirror), h′=+3 cmh' = +3\ \text{cm}h′=+3 cm — virtual, erect, diminished. (b) He gets v=+60v = +60v=+60 cm and m=+3m = +3m=+3 (an enlarged image) — impossible for a convex mirror, which always gives a diminished image; fff must be +30 cm.

    Common trap: Trusting any answer that "comes out". Always compare with the image rules.

Concept used: lens formula with f<0f < 0f<0; m=vum = \dfrac{v}{u}m=uv​ (Topic 7). Why it applies: uuu, fff, hhh are known.

    Sign table.

    Description and use

    Image between F2F_2F2​ and 2F22F_22F2​; diminished; real and inverted.

    A camera needs a real image (to fall on the sensor) that is smaller than the scene — exactly this case.

P21●● StandardDiagram-based · 3 marksOriginal

Ravi drew a ray diagram for an object placed between P and F of a concave mirror. His teacher marked four errors:

  1. none of the rays has an arrowhead;
  2. the lines behind the mirror are drawn solid, with arrowheads;
  3. the ray that came in parallel to the axis was reflected through a point labelled F behind the mirror;
  4. he wrote "image: real, enlarged".

Explain what is wrong in each and how to correct it.

Full solution

Given: four errors in a concave-mirror ray diagram (object inside F). Asked: the reason each is wrong and the correction.

Concept used: ray-diagram conventions and the concave-mirror image for an object inside F (Topic 2). Why it applies: each error breaks one convention or rule.

  1. 5

    No arrowheads: without arrows the direction of light is not shown. Correct: arrowheads on every real ray, before and after reflection.

  2. 6

    Solid lines behind the mirror: no light travels behind a mirror; these lines only show where rays seem to come from. Correct: draw backward extensions dashed, with no arrowheads.

  3. 7

    F behind the mirror: for a concave mirror, F is in front, halfway between P and C. Correct: the parallel ray reflects through F in front of the mirror.

  4. 8

    "Real": for an object inside F the reflected rays diverge and only their extensions meet, behind the mirror. Correct: "behind the mirror; enlarged; virtual and erect".

  5. Check: the corrected diagram matches the last row of the concave-mirror table ✔.

  6. Answer (1) Add arrowheads to all real rays. (2) Draw extensions behind the mirror dashed, without arrows. (3) F of a concave mirror is in front of it — reflect the parallel ray through that F. (4) The image is virtual and erect (and enlarged), behind the mirror.

P22●● StandardDiagram-based · 3 marksOriginal

(a) Draw the path of a ray of light that strikes a rectangular glass slab at an angle of incidence of 45°. Mark the angle of incidence, the angle of refraction and the angle of emergence, and show the lateral shift. (b) What is the angle of emergence? (c) How would the lateral shift change if a thicker slab were used?

Full solution

Given: glass slab; i=45°i = 45°i=45°. Asked: labelled diagram; angle of emergence; effect of thickness.

Concept used: refraction at two parallel faces (Topic 5, Practical 11). Why it applies: towards the normal on entering, away on leaving, equal and opposite.

  1. 1

    (a) How to draw it

    Draw the rectangular slab ABCD with a ruler.

  2. 2

    Draw the incident ray to a point O on face AB, and the normal at O (dashed, at 90° to AB). Make ∠i=45°\angle i = 45°∠i=45° with the normal.

  3. 3

    Inside the slab draw the refracted ray OO′ bending towards the normal (for ordinary glass, ∠r≈28°\angle r \approx 28°∠r≈28°).

  4. 4

    At O′ on face CD draw the normal (dashed). Draw the emergent ray bending away from the normal, parallel to the incident ray; mark ∠e\angle e∠e.

  5. 5

    Extend the incident ray through the slab as a dotted line; mark the perpendicular gap between it and the emergent ray as the lateral shift.

  6. 6

    (b)

    The faces are parallel, so ∠e=∠i=45°\angle e = \angle i = 45°∠e=∠i=45°.

  7. 7

    (c)

    The ray travels a longer path inside a thicker slab before it comes out, so the sideways gap grows: the lateral shift increases.

  8. Check: the emergent ray is parallel to, but not in line with, the incident ray ✔.

  9. Answer (a) Diagram as described (towards the normal at AB, away at CD, emergent ∥ incident, lateral shift marked). (b) 45° (c) The lateral shift increases.

P24●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Using the ray rules, explain why a convex mirror can never form a real image.

Full solution

Given: a convex mirror. Asked: why its image is never real.

Concept used: a real image needs reflected rays that actually meet in front of the mirror (Topic 1, Topic 3). Why it applies: we check how a convex mirror reflects rays.

  1. 1

    A ray parallel to the axis reflects away from the axis (as if from F behind the mirror).

  2. 2

    A ray aimed at C reflects back along itself, also moving away from the first ray.

  3. 3

    Every pair of reflected rays from a convex mirror diverges, so they never meet in front of the mirror.

  4. 4

    Only their backward extensions meet — behind the mirror — giving a virtual image.

  5. Check: consistent with both rows of the convex-mirror table (always virtual) ✔.

  6. Answer The bulging surface always makes the reflected rays spread out; they never actually meet, so no real image forms — only their backward extensions meet behind the mirror, giving a virtual image.

P25●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AA ray of light entering a glass slab along the normal does not bend.
RThe speed of light does not change when light enters glass along the normal.
refraction changes direction only for oblique rays; speed changes whenever the medium changes (Topic 5). Why it applies: we test each statement separately.

Given: an assertion and a reason about normal incidence. Asked: the correct option.

Concept used: refraction changes direction only for oblique rays; speed changes whenever the medium changes (Topic 5). Why it applies: we test each statement separately.

  1. 1

    A: a ray along the normal (i=0°i = 0°i=0°) goes straight through — true.

  2. 2

    R: light slows down in glass whatever the angle — false.

  3. 3

    A is true because the angle is zero, not because the speed stays the same.

  4. Check: Snell's law: sin⁡0°=0\sin 0° = 0sin0°=0, so sin⁡r=0\sin r = 0sinr=0 and r=0°r = 0°r=0°, even though n≠1n \ne 1n=1 ✔.

  5. Answer (C) A is true but R is false.

P36●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

The two laws of refraction

(a) State the two laws of refraction of light. (2)
(b) A ray of light passes from air into a rectangular glass slab. Name the angle of incidence, the angle of refraction and the normal on a labelled sketch, and say which way the ray bends. (1)

Full solution

Given: a ray going from air into glass. Asked: the two laws, and a labelled sketch with the direction of bending.

Concept used: the laws of refraction (Topic 5). Why it applies: they describe every ray that crosses from one transparent medium into another.

  1. 1

    First law: the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

  2. 2

    Second law (Snell's law): for a given pair of media and a given colour of light, sin⁡isin⁡r\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}sinrsini​ is a constant (the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first).

  3. 3

    Sketch: draw the air–glass surface, a dashed normal at the point where the ray enters, the incident ray in air, and the refracted ray in glass. Mark ∠i\angle i∠i between the incident ray and the normal, and ∠r\angle r∠r between the refracted ray and the normal.

  4. 4

    Bending: glass is optically denser than air, so the ray slows down and bends towards the normal (∠r<∠i\angle r < \angle i∠r<∠i).

  5. Check: both angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface ✔.

  6. Answer (a) The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; sin⁡isin⁡r\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}sinrsini​ is constant for a given pair of media and colour of light. (b) Sketch as described; the ray bends towards the normal.

    Common trap: Measuring iii and rrr from the glass surface instead of from the normal. Also, stating Snell's law without "for a given pair of media and colour of light" loses the mark in the exam.

In the lab (CBSE Practical 10), Isha points a convex lens at a building about 100 m away, seen through the window. She gets the sharpest image on a screen 20.2 cm from the lens.

(b) Is the true focal length slightly more or slightly less than 20.2 cm? Why? (1)
(c) Taking f=20f = 20f=20 cm, where must she put the screen to get a sharp image of a candle placed 30 cm from the lens? (1)
(d) Describe the candle's image. (1)

Full solution

Given: sharp image of a distant building at 20.2 cm; then f=20f = 20f=20 cm and a candle at 30 cm. Asked: parts (a)–(d).

Concept used: light from a distant object is nearly parallel, so its image forms almost at F; lens formula and m=vum = \dfrac{v}{u}m=uv​ (Topic 6, Topic 7). Why it applies: this is how Practical 10 measures focal length.

  1. 1

    (a)

    The building is very far away, so the image forms (almost) at F2F_2F2​: f ≈ 20.2 cm.

  2. 2

    (b)

    The building is not truly at infinity, so its image forms a little beyond F2F_2F2​.

  3. 3

    So the true focal length is slightly less than 20.2 cm.

  4. 4

    (c)

    Sign table.

    Quantity Value Reason for the sign
    uuu −30 cm-30\ \text{cm}−30 cm candle on the left
    fff +20 cm+20\ \text{cm}+20 cm convex lens
    vvv ? to be found

    Substitute: 1v=1(+20 cm)+1(−30 cm)\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{(+20\ \text{cm})} + \dfrac{1}{(-30\ \text{cm})}v1​=(+20 cm)1​+(−30 cm)1​.

    LCM 60: 1v=3−260 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{3 - 2}{60\ \text{cm}}v1​=60 cm3−2​.

    Simplify: 1v=160 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{60\ \text{cm}}v1​=60 cm1​.

  9. 9

    Flip: v=+60v = +60v=+60 cm → screen 60 cm from the lens, on the other side.

  10. 9

    (d)

    Lens magnification: m=vum = \dfrac{v}{u}m=uv​.

  11. 10

    Substitute: m=(+60 cm)(−30 cm)m = \dfrac{(+60\ \text{cm})}{(-30\ \text{cm})}m=(−30 cm)(+60 cm)​.

    Simplify: m=−2m = -2m=−2.

  13. 12

    Negative and of size 2 → real, inverted, enlarged (2 times).

  14. Check: (b) with u=−10 000u = -10\,000u=−10000 cm and f=+20f = +20f=+20 cm, the image forms at about +20.04 cm — just beyond F ✔. (c) candle between F1F_1F1​ and 2F12F_12F1​ → image beyond 2F22F_22F2​ (60 > 40 cm) ✔.

  15. Answer (a) About 20.2 cm (b) Slightly less, because the building is not at infinity, so its image forms just beyond F (c) 60 cm from the lens (v=+60v = +60v=+60 cm) (d) Real, inverted, 2 times enlarged

    (b)

    Minus of a minus becomes plus.

    1v=−18 cm+112 cm\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{8\ \text{cm}} + \dfrac{1}{12\ \text{cm}}v1​=−8 cm1​+12 cm1​Swipe to see the whole equation →

    LCM 24.

    m=−(−24 cm)(−12 cm)m = -\dfrac{(-24\ \text{cm})}{(-12\ \text{cm})}m=−(−12 cm)(−24 cm)​Swipe to see the whole equation →

P33●●● AdvancedNumerical · 4 marksOriginal

A concave mirror has a focal length of 12 cm. Find both positions of an object for which the image is twice the size of the object. State the nature of the image in each case.

Full solution

Given: concave mirror, f=−12f = -12f=−12 cm; image size twice the object. Asked: two object positions; nature of each image.

Concept used: "twice the size" can mean m=−2m = -2m=−2 (real, inverted) or m=+2m = +2m=+2 (virtual, erect); mirror formula with m=−vum = -\dfrac{v}{u}m=−uv​ (Topic 4). Why it applies: a concave mirror can enlarge both outside and inside F.

  1. 1

    Case 1: real image, m=−2m = -2m=−2

    Sign table: f=−12f = -12f=−12 cm (concave), m=−2m = -2m=−2 (real → inverted), uuu = ?, vvv = ?

  2. 2

    Put m=−2m = -2m=−2 in m=−vum = -\dfrac{v}{u}m=−uv​: −2=−vu-2 = -\dfrac{v}{u}−2=−uv​, so v=2uv = 2uv=2u.

  3. 3

    Mirror formula with v=2uv = 2uv=2u: 12u+1u=1f\dfrac{1}{2u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}2u1​+u1​=f1​.

  4. 4

    LCM 2u2u2u: 1+22u=32u=1f\dfrac{1 + 2}{2u} = \dfrac{3}{2u} = \dfrac{1}{f}2u1+2​=2u3​=f1​.

  5. 5

    Cross-multiply: 2u=3f2u = 3f2u=3f.

  6. 6

    Substitute fff: 2u=3×(−12 cm)=−36 cm2u = 3 \times (-12\ \text{cm}) = -36\ \text{cm}2u=3×(−12 cm)=−36 cm.

  7. 7

    Divide by 2: u=−18u = -18u=−18 cm.

  8. 8

    Then v=2uv = 2uv=2u.

  9. 9

    Substitute: v=2×(−18 cm)v = 2 \times (-18\ \text{cm})v=2×(−18 cm).

  10. 10

    Simplify: v=−36v = -36v=−36 cm.

  11. 9

    Case 2: virtual image, m=+2m = +2m=+2

    Sign table: f=−12f = -12f=−12 cm, m=+2m = +2m=+2 (virtual → erect), uuu = ?, vvv = ?

  12. 10

    Put m=+2m = +2m=+2 in m=−vum = -\dfrac{v}{u}m=−uv​: +2=−vu+2 = -\dfrac{v}{u}+2=−uv​, so v=−2uv = -2uv=−2u.

  13. 11

    Mirror formula with v=−2uv = -2uv=−2u: 1−2u+1u=1f\dfrac{1}{-2u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}−2u1​+u1​=f1​.

  14. 12

    LCM 2u2u2u: −1+22u=12u=1f\dfrac{-1 + 2}{2u} = \dfrac{1}{2u} = \dfrac{1}{f}2u−1+2​=2u1​=f1​.

  15. 13

    Cross-multiply: 2u=f=−122u = f = -122u=f=−12 cm.

  16. 14

    Divide by 2: u=−6u = -6u=−6 cm.

  17. 15

    Then v=−2uv = -2uv=−2u.

  18. 16

    Substitute: v=−2×(−6 cm)v = -2 \times (-6\ \text{cm})v=−2×(−6 cm).

  19. 17

    Simplify: v=+12v = +12v=+12 cm.

  20. Check: case 1: 1(−36)+1(−18)=−336=−112\dfrac{1}{(-36)} + \dfrac{1}{(-18)} = -\dfrac{3}{36} = -\dfrac{1}{12}(−36)1​+(−18)1​=−363​=−121​ ✔ (object between F and C). Case 2: 112+1(−6)=−112\dfrac{1}{12} + \dfrac{1}{(-6)} = -\dfrac{1}{12}121​+(−6)1​=−121​ ✔ (object inside F).

  21. Answer Object 18 cm in front (u=−18u = -18u=−18 cm): image at v=−36v = -36v=−36 cm, real, inverted and enlarged (twice the size). Object 6 cm in front (u=−6u = -6u=−6 cm): image at v=+12v = +12v=+12 cm, virtual, erect and enlarged (twice the size).

P34●●● AdvancedDiagram-based · 4 marksOriginal

A 1 cm tall object is placed 9 cm from (a) a concave mirror of focal length 6 cm and (b) a convex lens of focal length 6 cm. Draw both ray diagrams. Then give two similarities and one difference between the images.

Full solution

Given: f = 6 cm for both (C or 2F2F2F at 12 cm); object 1 cm tall at 9 cm. Asked: two ray diagrams; similarities and a difference.

Concept used: concave mirror and convex lens are both converging; an object between F and C (or 2F2F2F) gives a real, inverted, enlarged image (Topic 2, Topic 6). Why it applies: 6 cm < 9 cm < 12 cm in both cases.

  1. 1

    (a) Concave mirror — how to draw it

    Axis, mirror, P; F at 6 cm and C at 12 cm in front.

  2. 2

    AB at 9 cm. Ray 1: parallel → through F. Ray 3: along the line from C through B → back on itself.

  3. 3

    The rays cross below the axis beyond C, in front of the mirror: A′B′ (solid, inverted).

  4. 4

    (b) Convex lens — how to draw it

    Axis, lens, O; F1F_1F1​, F2F_2F2​ at 6 cm; 2F12F_12F1​, 2F22F_22F2​ at 12 cm.

  5. 5

    AB at 9 cm. Ray 1: parallel → through F2F_2F2​. Ray 3: straight through O.

  6. 6

    The rays cross below the axis beyond 2F22F_22F2​, on the other side of the lens: A′B′ (solid, inverted).

  7. 7

    Comparison

    Similar: both images are real and inverted; both are enlarged (2 times, see check).

  8. 8

    Different: the mirror's image forms on the same side as the object (in front of the mirror); the lens's image forms on the opposite side.

  9. Check: mirror: 1v=−16+19=−118\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{9} = -\dfrac{1}{18}v1​=−61​+91​=−181​ → v=−18v = -18v=−18 cm, m=−2m = -2m=−2. Lens: 1v=16−19=118\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{6} - \dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{1}{18}v1​=61​−91​=181​ → v=+18v = +18v=+18 cm, m=−2m = -2m=−2 ✔ — same size, opposite sides.

  10. Answer Both images: real, inverted, 2 times enlarged (2 cm), 18 cm away. Difference: mirror — in front (object's side); lens — on the other side.

P35●●● AdvancedDiagram-based · 3 marksOriginal

A coin lies at the bottom of a bucket of water and appears raised. (a) Draw a ray diagram showing why. (b) If the water were replaced by the same depth of kerosene (n=1.44n = 1.44n=1.44; water n=1.33n = 1.33n=1.33), would the coin appear more raised or less raised? Explain.

Full solution

Given: coin under water; kerosene alternative. Asked: ray diagram; comparison.

Concept used: light from the coin bends away from the normal as it leaves the denser liquid; the eye traces the ray back in a straight line (Topic 5). Why it applies: the apparent position is where the bent rays seem to come from.

  1. 1

    (a) How to draw it

    Draw the water surface as a horizontal line and the coin at the bottom (O).

  2. 2

    Draw two rays from O going up at small angles to the vertical, reaching the surface.

  3. 3

    At each point draw the normal (dashed). In air, draw each ray bending away from the normal towards the eye (arrowheads).

  4. 4

    Extend the two rays in air backwards (dashed) into the water; they meet at I, above O. I is the coin's apparent position.

  5. 5

    (b)

    Kerosene (1.44) is optically denser than water (1.33).

  6. 6

    Leaving kerosene, light bends more away from the normal than when leaving water.

  7. 7

    The backward extensions meet even higher, so the coin appears more raised.

  8. Check: the larger the refractive index, the shallower a liquid looks (apparent depth ≈ real depth ÷ n for near-vertical viewing — beyond the syllabus) ✔.

  9. Answer (a) Diagram: rays bend away from the normal at the surface; extended back they meet above the coin. (b) More raised, because kerosene has a higher refractive index, so the rays bend more at the surface.

E9●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Light SA 20

Identify the device used as a spherical mirror or lens in following cases, when the image formed is virtual and erect in each case.
(a) Object is placed between device and its focus, image formed is enlarged and behind it.
(b) Object is placed between the focus and device, image formed is enlarged and on the same side as that of the object.
(c) Object is placed between infinity and device, image formed is diminished and between focus and optical centre on the same side as that of the object.
(d) Object is placed between infinity and device, image formed is diminished and between pole and focus, behind it.

Full solution

Given: four descriptions of virtual, erect images. Asked: the device in each.

Concept used: "behind it" → mirror; "same side as the object" → lens; "enlarged" → converging device with object inside F; "diminished" → diverging device (Topic 2, Topic 3, Topic 6). Why it applies: each clue narrows the choice.

  1. 1

    (a) Enlarged, behind → a mirror that enlarges → concave mirror.

  2. 2

    (b) Enlarged, same side as object → lens used as magnifier → convex lens.

  3. 3

    (c) Diminished, between focus and optical centre → concave lens.

  4. 4

    (d) Diminished, between pole and focus, behind → convex mirror.

  5. Check: "optical centre" belongs to lenses and "pole" to mirrors — a quick confirmation for (c) and (d) ✔.

  6. Answer (a) Concave mirror (b) Convex lens (c) Concave lens (d) Convex mirror

    f=+20 cmf = +20\ \text{cm}f=+20 cmSwipe to see the whole equation →

  9. Check: object at 26.7 cm lies between F1F_1F1​ (20 cm) and 2F12F_12F1​ (40 cm) → real, enlarged image beyond 2F22F_22F2​ (80 cm > 40 cm) ✔.

  10. Answer The candle is 803 cm≈26.7 cm\dfrac{80}{3}\ \text{cm} \approx 26.7\ \text{cm}380​ cm≈26.7 cm from the lens (u=−803u = -\dfrac{80}{3}u=−380​ cm). The image is real and inverted (3 times enlarged); the lens is convex (f=+20f = +20f=+20 cm).

E12●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 5 marksNCERT Exemplar Light LA 38

A student focussed the image of a candle flame on a white screen using a convex lens. He noted down the position of the candle, screen and the lens as under: Position of candle = 12.0 cm; Position of convex lens = 50.0 cm; Position of the screen = 88.0 cm.
(i) What is the focal length of the convex lens?
(ii) Where will the image be formed if he shifts the candle towards the lens at a position of 31.0 cm?
(iii) What will be the nature of the image formed if he further shifts the candle towards the lens?
(iv) Draw a ray diagram to show the formation of the image in case (iii) as said above.

Full solution

Given: optical-bench readings: candle 12.0 cm, lens 50.0 cm, screen 88.0 cm. Asked: (i)–(iv).

Concept used: distances are measured from the lens; a same-distance real image means the object is at 2F2F2F; lens formula (Topic 6, Topic 7). Why it applies: the readings are scale positions, not distances.

  1. 1

    (i)

    Candle-to-lens distance: 50.0 − 12.0 = 38.0 cm → u=−38.0u = -38.0u=−38.0 cm.

  2. 2

    Lens-to-screen distance: 88.0 − 50.0 = 38.0 cm → v=+38.0v = +38.0v=+38.0 cm.

  3. 3

    Equal distances → object and image at 2F2F2F, so 2f=38.02f = 38.02f=38.0 cm.

  4. 4

    f=19.0f = 19.0f=19.0 cm. (Lens formula check: 1f=138−1(−38)=238=119\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{38} - \dfrac{1}{(-38)} = \dfrac{2}{38} = \dfrac{1}{19}f1​=381​−(−38)1​=382​=191​ ✔.)

  5. 5

    (ii)

    New candle distance: 50.0 − 31.0 = 19.0 cm → u=−19.0u = -19.0u=−19.0 cm = −f-f−f: the candle is at F1F_1F1​.

  6. 6

    Rays from F1F_1F1​ come out parallel, so the image is formed at infinity (no sharp image on the screen).

  7. 7

    (iii)

    Moving the candle closer than F1F_1F1​ (less than 19 cm from the lens) gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image on the same side as the candle.

  8. 8

    (iv) How to draw it

    Axis, lens, O; F1F_1F1​, F2F_2F2​ at 19 cm. Candle AB between F1F_1F1​ and O.

  9. 9

    Ray 1: parallel → through F2F_2F2​. Ray 3: straight through O.

  10. 10

    Extend both refracted rays backwards (dashed); they meet on the candle's side, farther away than AB: A′B′ upright and larger (as in Topic 6 Worked example 2).

  11. Check: official key: (i) 19 cm, (ii) at infinity, (iii) virtual and erect ✔.

  12. Answer (i) f=19.0 cmf = 19.0\ \text{cm}f=19.0 cm (ii) At infinity (the candle is at the focus) (iii) Virtual, erect and enlarged, on the same side as the candle (iv) Ray diagram as described.

    Common trap: Using the scale readings (12.0 cm, 88.0 cm) directly as uuu and vvv. Subtract the lens position first.
